facts.statement: The researchers tested three specific MRI techniques to see if they could predict which way a brain tumor would grow after surgery.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Doctors looked at follow-up scans to determine if the tumor grew sideways, upward, downward, or in other directions away from the surgical site.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The diffusion anisotropy method correctly predicted the direction of tumor growth in about 75% of cases, outperforming the other two imaging methods.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Mixing the diffusion anisotropy data with the other imaging types did not make the prediction any better than using the diffusion anisotropy method by itself.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The study looked back at data from patients who had a specific aggressive brain tumor limited to the temporal lobe and who had their entire visible tumor removed.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors suggest this imaging tool could help surgeons plan operations by showing them the likely path of tumor growth before the surgery happens.
facts.subject: humans
